title: scotland spain canada grapple with wildfires 2026 07 21
text:
LONDON, July 21 (Reuters) - Hello,
Wildfires and air pollution in North America and Europe are the focus of today’s newsletter in a trend scientists have linked to climate change, as firefighters battle blazes in Scotland, Spain, France and Canada.
The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service
, opens new tab
 (SFRS) is tackling two wildfires, with one in the Glenmore area of the Cairngorms National Park which has burned since last Wednesday, with another grassfire on ​Arthur’s Seat in Edinburgh.
The SFRS and the Scottish Wildfire Forum issued a very high wildfire risk warning which has been extended until July 24.
In Spain, a wildfire raged ‌across the central Guadalajara province on Monday, burning for a fifth day and becoming the largest blaze of the year, as forecasters warned an approaching heatwave would raise fire risks across much of the country.
Meanwhile in France, local prefect Simon Babre told national news station BFMTV that a wildfire on the Mediterranean coast near Frejus "spread extremely quickly in the context of this heatwave and extreme drought". Train services between the Mediterranean port of Toulon and Les Arcs were suspended.
In Canada, Premier ​Doug Ford said at a press conference in Toronto that Ontario is battling 190 active blazes and around 1,800 residents had been evacuated from sparsely populated communities in the northwest of ​the province.
Spain’s largest wildfire
Spain is tackling one of its largest blazes of the year which comes less than two weeks after a wildfire near Bedar, ⁠in Almeria province, killed 13 people – one of Spain's deadliest blazes in decades.
Authorities evacuated three additional municipalities on Monday as the La Mierla wildfire in Guadalajara province expanded to more than 26,000 hectares (64,247 acres). ​More than 1,000 residents have been evacuated from their homes.
Spain's weather agency AEMET said the heatwave, the third of 2026, was expected to last at least until Thursday, bringing temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees ​Fahrenheit) across much of the southeastern interior and pushing wildfire danger to extreme levels.
Some areas could reach 42 to 44 C by Thursday as hot, dry air moves north from Africa. The agency also warned of possible dry thunderstorms in mountainous areas of eastern Spain.
Canada’s blazes and smoke
Heavy smoke from fires in northern and western Ontario as well as northern Minnesota brought the world's worst air quality to Toronto last week, which then spread to New York and Washington.
Air quality ​has since improved in southern Ontario as well as the U.S. Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, although it remained poor in several U.S. states in the Midwest. Click here for an explainer on why the wildfires ​spread over from Canada to the United States.
The wildfires, which are mostly in difficult-to-access areas, have increased tensions between Canada and the U.S., where some politicians have criticized Canada's response.
U.S. President Donald Trump said that he told Canadian ‌Prime Minister Mark ⁠Carney that Canada must do better at controlling Ontario wildfires.
Trump said he spoke to Carney about the issue at the FIFA World Cup Final on Sunday, two days after threatening to levy tariffs on Canadian goods to punish Canada over the wildfire smoke.
Carney has not directly responded to Trump, although he has said all countries including the U.S. must do more to address climate change.
Ford said it's "unacceptable" that Trump has chosen to criticize Canada's wildfire response and threaten tariffs rather than sending help.
Major fires have become a regular occurrence in Canada, home to some of the world's largest forests. Climate experts say rising temperatures have led ​to drier timber and increased fire risk.
In ​Conversation
Jane Burston, CEO of global philanthropic organization Clean ⁠Air Fund, shares her thoughts on air pollution amid increasing wildfires in Europe:
“The wildfires raging across the UK and wider Europe risk taking lives long after the flames have subsided due to the vast air pollution they generate.
“Wildfires throw huge amounts of black carbon, commonly known as soot, into the atmosphere. This ​contributes to respiratory illnesses and cardiovascular diseases and is a major cause of the 7.9 million premature deaths annually attributed to air pollution.
“Black carbon is ​also one of the super-pollutants ⁠causing nearly half of global warming, creating a vicious circle where wildfires damage our health while simultaneously making future wildfires more likely.
“This cycle is not inevitable; we can break it with tighter regulation of super pollutants like black carbon, alongside robust fire prevention procedures, early warning systems and support for local authorities to strengthen their emergency responses.
“Every wildfire we can prevent will help to save lives now while safeguarding our climate, cleaning our air ⁠and protecting ​generations to come.”
ESG Spotlight
Today’s spotlight brings us a lesson in climate resilience training as a centre in eastern China teaches citizens ​how to survive extreme weather events.
Lvxing Disaster Simulation Training Center in Hangzhou offers a realistic experience of what it is like to be caught up in a typhoon or a flash flood, albeit with the advantage of wearing a wetsuit, a helmet and ​having a safety instructor.
